Newborn Cuvier's beaked whales are among the largest cetacean neonates relative to maternal size, with a length at birth of 210 centimeters [Lb = 210 centimeters], a value that reflects the precocial developmental state of the calf. These neonates emerge after a substantial gestation period estimated at approximately 365 days [tg = approximately 365 days], based on comparative data from the related northern bottlenose whale Hyperoodon ampullatus and adjusted for body size, under a core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. The dependent calf then undergoes a prolonged suckling phase, and the time elapsed from birth to the cessation of nursing is similarly inferred to be about 365 days [tx = about 365 days] at the same internal tempe at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]rature. This extended period of maternal investment, characteristic of deep-diving ziphiids, is thought to enable the juvenile to accumulate sufficient lipid reserves and develop the physiological capacity for the extreme foraging dives that define the species' ecological niche in the mesopelagic zone.

As females approach sexual maturation, considerable somatic growth is required before reproductive activity can commence. Field observations and examination of stranding records indicate that the length at which puberty is attained is approximately 650 centimeters [Lp = approximately 650 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to the onset of follicular development and the potential for ovulation. This length is notably intermediate between the dimensions of the newborn and the fully mature adult, underscoring the substantial growth trajectory that characterizes the life history of this species. The ultimate length for females, representing the maximum asymptotic body size attained by adult individuals, has been estimated at approximately 740 centimeters [Li = approximately 740 centimeters], consistent with measurements from adult female specimens examined in the field and from stranded individuals along the California coastline. This terminal size is broadly consistent with the few reliable data available for the genus Ziphius.

The maximum body mass that a fully grown adult female can achieve, known as the ultimate wet weight, is estimated to be approximately 3.25 million grams [Wwi = approximately 3.25 million grams], placing this species among the heavier members of the Ziphiidae family. This mass, equivalent to roughly 3.25 metric tons, is consistent with the robust, fusiform body plan that facilitates efficient locomotion during deep, prolonged foraging dives that can exceed depths of two kilometers. The substantial weight of the adult female reflects the energetic reserves required to support both the demanding deep-diving lifestyle and the metabolic costs of gestation and lactation. In comparison to other beaked whales of similar body length, this wet weight aligns with predictions based on length-weight regressions for the genus Ziphius, and it provides a critical baseline for estimating the metabolic requirements and food intake needed to sustain such a large-bodied, endothermic marine predator in the oligotrophic waters it often inhabits.

The maximum lifespan for Cuvier's beaked whale, inferred from the analysis of growth layer groups in the teeth of stranded specimens and calibrated for a core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], is estimated to be approximately 22,630 days [am = approximately 22,630 days], which corresponds to roughly 62 years. This remarkable longevity, one of the highest recorded among odontocetes, is thought to be linked to the species' extremely slow pace of life and delayed reproductive schedule, which are adaptations to the unpredictable and energy-poor deep-sea environment. The pronounced lifespan likely allows females multiple reproductive opportunities across their long adult lives, offsetting the significant energetic investment required for each single calf. When compared to the closely related Hyperoodon ampullatus, which also exhibits considerable longevity, this extended lifespan supports the hypothesis that slow life histories are a conserved trait within the Ziphiidae family, driven by the ecological constraints of deep-diving, low-metabolism foraging strategies.

Under the stable thermal conditions of a deep-diving mammal's core body temperature, which is maintained at approximately 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Cuvier's beaked whale has been inferred from comparative life history data for Hyperoodon ampullatus. Available evidence suggests that the effective annual birth rate is roughly one calf every two years [Ri = roughly one calf every two years]. This slow reproductive pace, yielding an effective annual birth rate of about 0.5 calves per year, is characteristic of a species that invests heavily in each offspring through a long gestation and an extended period of lactation and maternal care. The prolonged interval between successive births is thought to be a direct consequence of the energetic demands imposed by deep foraging dives, which limit the female's ability to simultaneously sustain a rapidly growing fetus or suckling calf while meeting her own metabolic needs in the food-scarce mesopelagic environment.
